subject: Biotechnology
title: Constructed Wetlands
description: A fast breakdown of Constructed Wetlands for builders.

hook.text: A swamp that cleans sewage — constructed wetlands use plants, soil, and microbes to treat wastewater without machines.

buildup.text: Wetland plants like reeds and cattails transport oxygen to their roots — creating aerobic zones where bacteria degrade pollutants.

discovery.text: Biofilm on gravel and roots hosts diverse microbial communities — performing nitrification, denitrification, and organic decay.

twist.text: Constructed wetlands need large land areas — ten times more space than conventional treatment plants for the same capacity.

climax.text: Vertical flow wetlands stack treatment stages — reducing the footprint while maintaining natural treatment effectiveness.

punchline.text: Nature's water filter — constructed wetlands treat sewage with plants, not pumps.

quiz.question: What is the main disadvantage of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment?
options: They cannot remove nitrogen or organic pollutants
They require about ten times more land area than conventional treatment plants
They only work in tropical climates

details.summary: Constructed wetlands are engineered ecosystems using plants, soil, and microbial communities to treat wastewater naturally. Water flows through planted beds where roots, biofilms, and anaerobic zones remove pollutants through physical, chemical, and biological processes simultaneously.
details.whyItMatters: Constructed wetlands provide effective wastewater treatment with minimal energy input and operational costs, making them ideal for developing communities and rural areas.
takeaways: Plant roots and microbial biofilms remove pollutants from flowing wastewater
They require minimal energy and maintenance compared to conventional treatment
Wetlands simultaneously treat water, create habitat, and provide green space

faq.question: How do constructed wetlands remove pollutants from water?
faq.answer: Plants absorb nutrients and some metals through roots. Microbial communities on root surfaces and in gravel media degrade organic pollutants. Anaerobic zones enable nitrogen removal through denitrification. Physical filtration through substrate material removes suspended solids and pathogens.

faq.question: What types of pollution can constructed wetlands treat?
faq.answer: They effectively treat sewage, agricultural runoff, stormwater, mine drainage, and some industrial wastewater. They remove organic matter, nutrients, pathogens, some metals, and certain pharmaceuticals. Complex industrial chemicals may require pretreatment before wetland polishing.
